items.text: A gunman killed six people and wounded at least 15 in Kraków's Main Market Square on Saturday; Poland's defense minister called it an act of terror.
items.detail: Police said the 25-year-old Polish suspect drove to several spots around the square in Kraków's Old Town shortly after 3 p.m. local time and opened fire with an automatic weapon at each stop before officers shot and wounded him; he is hospitalized after surgery. Four women and two men were killed; police said at least one victim was British. Two police officers were among the wounded. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect was fascinated by far-right ideologies and held "ultranationalistic" views, and that he may have taken the weapons from his family's home, where his father held gun permits. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Saturday evening that two women and a man were found dead in the suspect's home and were likely close family members. Authorities said there is no indication of a second attacker.
items.why: It is one of the deadliest mass shootings in modern Polish history, in the heart of a major European tourist city.

items.text: President Trump said he is ordering the Justice Department to investigate Democratic leaders over what he called threats against Republicans.
items.detail: In a Truth Social post Saturday, Trump said Democrats were "threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General," with impeachment and other punishment, called it "extortion at the highest level" and wrote, "I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!" He did not identify the "threatening letters" he cited, who sent them or who received them, and gave no evidence of a crime. He singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan. The White House and Slotkin did not immediately comment, and the Justice Department has not announced an investigation.
items.why: It comes days after Democrats won both chambers and are signaling oversight of the administration.

items.text: The U.S. military disabled a cargo ship trying to break the Iran blockade and set up a new task force to choke Iran's land and Caspian routes.
items.detail: U.S. Central Command said a U.S. aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of the St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday after its crew ignored repeated warnings and tried to leave the region following a call at an Iranian port; the crew had been told to leave the targeted spaces. CENTCOM said blockade enforcement since July has redirected 147 vessels and disabled five that refused to comply. Separately, CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper ordered the formation of Task Force Iron Gate, a staff of about 20 civilian and military personnel in Tampa that will work with other agencies to stop weapons, dual-use technology, sanctioned goods and illicit revenue from moving across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea. CENTCOM estimates the naval blockade has kept Iran from exporting more than $25 billion in crude oil. Also Saturday, Iran's Revolutionary Guard spokesman said the country had lifted its self-imposed 2,000-kilometer limit on missile range.
items.why: Washington is widening its pressure on Iran from the sea to land routes as fears of a renewed war rise.

items.text: Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main challenger, will get the first chance to form Israel's next government, President Isaac Herzog announced Saturday.
items.detail: Herzog informed Eisenkot and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of his decision Saturday evening and will formally hand Eisenkot the mandate at a ceremony Sunday. Eisenkot, a former military chief who leads the Yashar party, was recommended by parties representing 67 lawmakers, against 46 for Netanyahu. He has 28 days to build a coalition of at least 61 of the Knesset's 120 seats, with a possible 14-day extension. His four-party bloc won 48 seats in the Oct. 27 election and Netanyahu's bloc 53. Earlier Saturday, Netanyahu called for a national unity government.
items.why: It is the closest Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, has come to losing power since 2021.

items.text: The Justice Department is joining Texas' $1.8 billion Medicaid-fraud lawsuit against Planned Parenthood, according to a court filing.
items.detail: The department said in a filing late Friday that it intends to intervene in the 2021 False Claims Act case in federal court in Amarillo, brought by outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and an anonymous whistleblower. The suit says Planned Parenthood kept billing Texas and Louisiana Medicaid after the states moved to cut it off and did not repay the money once the terminations took effect; the plaintiffs seek about $1.8 billion in repayments and penalties. Planned Parenthood says the billing was legal while courts had paused the terminations, has said a loss would force it to shut down in Texas, and said Saturday it will fight the case at trial, expected in 2027. The Justice Department under President Biden declined to join the case in 2021. The filing came days after Texans elected Democrat Nathan Johnson as the next attorney general.
items.why: Federal backing raises the stakes in a case Planned Parenthood says could close its Texas clinics.
items.source: U.S. District Court, N.D. Texas (docket) / Reuters

items.text: Airstrikes on a village near Yemen's capital killed at least 27 people, mostly women and children, the Houthi-run health ministry said, blaming Saudi Arabia.
items.detail: The ministry said the strikes Saturday hit homes in Bani Hushaysh, a Houthi stronghold east of Sanaa, and wounded 36. A Sanaa hospital director said many victims, including first responders, remained under rubble. The toll could not be independently verified; Saudi Arabia did not immediately comment. It is one of the deadliest reported attacks since fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed in July as a spillover of the U.S.-Iran conflict, shattering a 2022 U.N.-brokered truce.
items.why: The renewed Saudi-Houthi war is deepening one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

items.text: UFC chief Dana White was offered the White House press secretary job, President Trump said Saturday; it is unclear whether White accepted.
items.detail: Trump wrote on Truth Social that White "has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States" and asked him to bring current and former UFC fighters as assistants. White then posted an image of himself behind the briefing-room lectern on Instagram with the caption "On to the next chapter." The White House and UFC did not immediately comment. The post has been vacant since Katie Zacharia left in October, five days after succeeding Karoline Leavitt. It follows Friday's announcement that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff.
items.why: It is the latest move in a White House staff shake-up after the midterm losses.

items.text: A federal judge plans to appoint former U.S. Attorney Jessie Liu to investigate whether officials misled the court over Trump's East Potomac golf course project.
items.detail: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said Saturday that Liu, who was D.C.'s top federal prosecutor in Trump's first term, would examine as special master whether Interior Department, National Park Service and Justice Department officials violated ethics rules or misled her about the renovation plans and the cutting of hundreds of trees. Both sides have until Friday, when the next hearing is set, to respond. The administration plans to close the public course Nov. 15 for a 15-month rebuild; Reyes' injunction bars further tree removal while the case continues.
items.why: A court-appointed probe of government candor can lead to contempt findings.
